To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) an OSP architecture is needed to provide facilities to refer to and integrate e-Government services, (b) XML, WSDL and UDDI are key enabling technologies for the first two layers of such an OSP architecture and (c) workflow management and coordination technologies are needed to address the cross-organisatinal workflow issues.
the architecture of an one-stop service provider is a multi-layered one and that the enabling technologies for the different layers are quickly evolving.

(1) the layered approach to one-stop service offerings is the most promising one; (2) a combination of technologies is needed to realize the different layers of such an approach; (3) abstracting the service heterogeneity is the most important issue; (4) the workflow control issue can be solved with a hybrid style.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing an architectural framework for e-Government service integration, and with the development of a reference architecture that supports the implementation of such a framework.

developing an OSP architecture that is capable of providing a uniform way for referring, invoking and integrating e-Government services, in the context or cross-organisaton workflows, while taking into account the heterogeneity of these services.
the design of an OSP architecture, which is based on a layered approach, that allows for the integration of e-Government services and the control of cross-organizational workflows in a uniform way.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single solution, but that there are a number of options to be evaluated, each with its own merits and drawbacks.
, although many technologies are available, the issues of (a) and (b) have not been solved yet.
the technologies are there, but the issues are still unsolved.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the layered OSP architecture is feasible and that the two major issues can be solved by a suitable combination of technologies.
, although there is a wide range of enabling technologies for the OSP architecture, there is a lack of standardisation in the areas of workflow management and cross-organisatinal service integration.
we are convinced that an architecture for one-stop service provision can be built on the available technologies and that the issues mentioned are solvable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to provide one-stop services, a number of technologies need to be integrated, which is not an easy task.

the OSP architecture should be designed to be flexible enough to support a wide variety of cross-organizational workflows, and that a combination of peer-to-peer and centralised workflow control styles is most promising.

, although many of the technologies required for the OSP architecture are already in place and are quickly evolving, the issues of service abstraction and cross-organisatioanl workflow control still need to be addressed.
